question: A 16-year-old male is brought to the clinic by his mother for the complaints of fever, nonproductive cough, fatigue, lack of appetite, and sore throat for the past 2 months.  Several other students at his high school have had similar symptoms. Physical exam shows a whitish membrane in his oropharynx, bilateral enlarged cervical lymphadenopathy, and mild splenomegaly.  Which of the following tests is most likely to diagnose his condition.?
analysis: The symptoms presented by the 16-year-old male, including fever, nonproductive cough, fatigue, sore throat, and the presence of a whitish membrane in the oropharynx, along with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and mild splenomegaly, are suggestive of infectious mononucleosis, commonly caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The Monospot test is a heterophile antibody test that is commonly used to diagnose infectious mononucleosis. Other options such as throat culture, chest X-ray, urine culture, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) are not the first-line tests for this condition. Therefore, the Monospot test is the most appropriate diagnostic test in this scenario.
